Mahinda Yapa Abeywardena then contested for Southern Provincial Council under DUNF and won. He was then elected as the opposition leader of the Southern Provincial Council in 1993, and he became the Chief Minister of the Southern Provincial Council in 1994. Elected twice as the Chief Minister he was in office from 1994 to 2001. He is said to be one of the most successful Chief Ministers from south for developing the infrastructures that was neglected for more than 5 years due to the dark era of the country. He left office to contest in 2001 general elections and become an opposition MP and served till 2004. After 2004 General elections, he became the Deputy Minister of Healthcare and later the Cabinet Minister for Cultural Affairs & National Heritage. After 2010 General Elections, he was Appointed as the Minister of Agriculture. Having been in office as the Minister of Agriculture for several years he was elected Vice Chairman at the 38th session of the Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations FAO Conference held in Rome, Italy in 2013. He was again appointed as the Minister of Parliamentary Affairs in 2015 for a brief period until he resigned and joined the opposition. He is a representative of Matara District for the United People's Freedom Alliance in the Parliament of Sri Lanka. He resides in Kalubowila, Dehiwala.

Mahidol Adulyadej (1892-1929) was former prince and a member of the Thai royal family. He was the father of Thai kings Ananda Mahidol (Rama VIII) and Bhumibol Adulyadej (Rama IX). He is known as the Father of modern medicine and public health in Thailand. His Royal Highness Prince Mahidol Adulyadej Vikrom, the Father of Modern Medicine in Thailand. His Royal Highness Prince Mahidol Adulyadej Vikrom, the Royal Father, was the 69th son of His Majesty King Chulalongkorn and the 7th son of Her Majesty Queen Sri Savarindira, the Queen Mother. He was born on Friday, the 3rd day of the 2nd lunar month, in the Year of the Rabbit, corresponding to January 1, 1891, in the Grand Palace. In 1903, at the age of 12, His Majesty the King...His Majesty King Chulalongkorn issued a royal decree establishing His Royal Highness Prince Mahidol Adulyadej as His Royal Highness the Crown Prince, with the official name as inscribed on the golden plaque: "His Royal Highness Prince Mahidol Adulyadej Naresuan Maharatathibodin Chulalongkornthrachavangkun Somboonbenjapornsiri." Sawad Khatiya Ropatosuchat Kunsangkas Kiatprakrit Lakshana Vichitpisitburut Chanudomratphat His Royal Highness Prince Sakdi Akkharat Worakuman, Krom Khun Songkhla Nakarin, with the name Musikan, was granted a rank of 40,000 according to the royal decree, similar to that of a Somdej Phra Chao Luk Ya Thoe Chao Fa Krom Khun Songkhla Nakarin. In 1904, he was ordained as a novice monk. At Wat Phra Sri Rattanasasadaram, His Royal Highness Prince Vajirayanavarorasa, the Supreme Patriarch, served as the Royal Preceptor, residing at the royal residence within Wat Bowonniwet Vihara. He left the monastic life on December 13, 1904, and in the same year, he went to study at Harrow School in London, England, until 1907. He then transferred to study military science at the Junior Military Academy in Potsdam, Germany, and the Higher Military Academy at Gross-Lichterfelde in Berlin, Germany. He completed his education. He studied military science in the army and passed the exam to become a Fenrich. (Fähnrich) was a student who scored exceptionally well; he wrote and composed essays so well that he didn't need to take an oral exam. Approximately 400 students took the exam...Only one person scored the same as him, making him the first Thai person to achieve the highest score in the examination. Afterward, he switched from army studies to naval studies because the Siamese army at that time lacked many qualified naval officers. He studied naval science at the Flensburg-Mürwik Naval Academy, as part of the 1912 class (CREW 1912), and graduated with excellent results in both theory and practice. In 1914, he returned to Thailand and was granted the rank of Lieutenant Commander. In 1915, he entered service as a reserve officer in the Naval General Staff Department. Later, he transferred to the Naval Academy Instructor Division, Textbook Writing Section, Naval Education Department. In 1916, he resigned from the Royal Thai Navy to study public health at the School for Health Officers, Harvard University, USA. After completing his pre-clinical medical studies, he temporarily suspended his medical studies and enrolled in a public health school established jointly by Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 1919. During his studies, he authored a research report entitled "A sanitary survey of the city of Gloucester, Massachusetts 1921" and graduated with a diploma in public health in 1921. While studying at Harvard University, he rented an apartment and had one servant. He used the name "Mr. Mahidol Songkhla". While studying in the United States, His Majesty granted scholarships to two medical students to study in the United States. The medical school selected two students: Sangwan Talaphat (later Her Majesty Queen Sri Savangavadhana) and Ubol Palakawong na Ayutthaya (later Ubol Lipithamsriphayat). His Majesty the King cared for both of his students diligently, providing them with guidance on life, customs, and traditions of the foreign country. While studying public health in his third year, His Majesty the King returned to attend the cremation ceremony of Her Majesty Queen Sri Patcharin, the Queen Mother. On October 10, 1920, His Majesty the King married Miss Sangwan Talaphat (later Her Majesty Queen Sri Savangavadhana). In 1926, he went to study medicine. Continuing on, at Harvard University in the United States, until...Until he graduated and received a degree. Medical Doctor, Cum Laude (Honors). In 1928, he returned to Thailand on December 13, 1928, and served as a resident physician at McCormick Hospital in Chiang Mai. He became a member of the Medical Association and treated general patients. He served as a resident for only three weeks before having to return to Bangkok to attend the royal cremation ceremony of Prince Bhanuphanuwongse. After that, he became ill, and his condition worsened until he passed away on September 24, 1929, at the age of 37 years, 8 months, and 23 days. King Prajadhipok issued a royal decree... In 1970, he was bestowed the title of "His Royal Highness the Father," and on June 9, 1970, he was granted the royal title "His Royal Highness Prince Mahidol Adulyadej Vikrom, the Royal Father." 2. Personal Life (Name and Royal Surname Mahidol) The original name of His Royal Highness Prince Mahidol Adulyadej Vikrom, the Royal Father, can be found in two forms: Mahidol Aduldej and Mahidol Adulyadej. Initially, King Chulalongkorn bestowed upon him the name "Mahidol Aduldej" during the one-month celebration. Later, when he reached the age of 12, King Chulalongkorn graciously ordered a royal tonsure ceremony and granted him a royal decree. At the same time, he was elevated to the rank of Prince of the Songkhla region, with the name inscribed on the royal decree as "Mahidol Adulyadej". Later, when King Prajadhipok graciously elevated his title to "Krom Luang Songkhla Nakarin," and when King Ananda Mahidol ascended the throne as the eighth monarch of the Chakri Dynasty, his name as inscribed on the royal golden plaque reverted to "Mahidol Aduldej." In 1970, His Majesty King Bhumibol Adulyadej the Great issued a royal decree posthumously bestowing the title "Somdej Phra Mahitalathibes Adulyadej Vikrom Phra Boromrajchanok" upon the remains of his royal father. Currently, his name is commonly written as "Mahidol Adulyadej." As for his surname, while studying abroad, he used the name Mr. Mahidol Songkla, and Her Majesty Queen Sri Savangavadhana used Mrs. Songkla. Therefore, his sons and daughters use the surname "Songkhla." Later, in 1970, King Prajadhipok granted a surname to descendants of the fifth generation of the royal family. In 1929, members of the royal family descended from His Royal Highness Prince Mahidol Adulyadej Vikrom, the Royal Father, were permitted to use the surname "Mahidol," which remains to this day. His Royal Highness Prince Mahidol Adulyadej Vikrom, the Royal Father, married Her Royal Highness Princess Srinagarindra, the Royal Mother, and they had three children: - Her Royal Highness Princess Galyani Vadhana, Krom Luang Narathiwat Rajanagarindra - His Majesty King Ananda Mahidol, Rama VIII - His Majesty King Bhumibol Adulyadej the Great, Rama IX. During his time serving in the Royal Thai Navy, His Majesty King Bhumibol Adulyadej initiated a submarine project. Although it was not fulfilled at that time, 20 years later, the Royal Thai Navy ordered the construction of four submarines: HTMS Matchanu, HTMS Wirun, HTMS Sinsamut, and HTMS Phlai Chumphon. In addition to submarines, His Majesty also drafted a plan for building a comprehensive naval force. Currently, the Royal Thai Navy has established naval bases and naval stations, and deployed naval forces to these bases and stations, in accordance with His Majesty's vision for building a full naval fleet. In the field of medicine, throughout the 10 years that His Majesty was involved in the medical field, he performed numerous royal duties. He dedicated both his royal wealth, his physical and mental strength to medicine, namely, granting funds for education and research, and providing royal funds for the construction of various buildings and the expansion of Siriraj Hospital. In the field of public health, His Majesty had surveyed Sanitation in Bangkok, for comparison with other countries that His Majesty studied, was helped to train the students. The provincial public health department had previously expressed a desire to have cremations performed electrically in order to comply with the regulations. In addition to the sanitation course, His Majesty also showed his compassion by assisting with education in other fields. Beyond medicine, for example, His Majesty granted a scholarship of 100,000 baht to send people to study abroad in fisheries and aquaculture for the betterment of Thai nutrition, earning him the title "The Guiding Light of Thai Aquatic Conservation." He also granted funds to Bangkok Christian College to hire foreign teachers, donated money to McCormick Hospital to purchase an X-ray machine, and provided financial support to Songkhla Hospital yearly. He studied at the Royal Prussian Military Preparatory College and the Imperial Military Academy in Germany. Later In 1916, he went to the United States to study public health at Harvard University. He earned a certificate in public health in 1921. In 1920, he married Princess Srinagarindra. He died in 1929 at the age of 37 due to kidney disease.

Mahidevran Sultan (; about 1499 – 3 February 1581) also called Gülbahar Sultan, (, meaning "spring rose"), the chief consort and Haseki Sultanof Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent of the Ottoman Empire and the mother of Şehzade Mustafa. She was known for her beauty, pride, and as the mother of the Sultan’s eldest son, which gave her respect in the palace and a special role in the harem. Her life shows the influence that mothers of princes had in the Ottoman court, as well as the rivalries between women for the Sultan’s attention. The name Mahidevran means “moon of fortune” or “one whose beauty never fades”. The name is of Persian origin and reflects the poetic naming traditions commonly used for women of the Ottoman imperial harem. Her birth name is not recorded in contemporary Ottoman sources. It was customary for women entering the imperial harem to be given new Persian or Arabic names, often replacing their original names from their place of origin. Some later traditions refer to her as Gülbahar, although historians note that this identification is uncertain and may result from confusion with other Ottoman consorts who bore the same name. Mahidevran was the mother of Şehzade Mustafa, the eldest surviving son of the Sultan. She had an important position in her son's harem in Manisa. While Hürrem Sultan became Suleiman's favorite and legal wife, Mahidevran kept the special status of being the mother of the eldest son, and some diplomats called her Suleiman's "first wife" even though they were never married. Before Hürrem was given the title of "Sultan" and later "Haseki Sultan", all women in the harem were called "Hatun", meaning "lady" or "woman". So Mahidevran never had the title of Sultana and was called simply "Mahidevran Hatun". Even so, she was respected as the mother of the eldest son. In books and historical fiction, she is sometimes wrongly called Sultan.Sometimes, she is also incorrectly called Baş Kadın, but this title did not exist in the 16th century. Her origins are unknown, and different historians have attributed various ethnic backgrounds to her. She has been described as Circassian, Albanian, Montenegrin, or of Crimean origin. According to an interview with Saide Perizat Temrukoğlu, an apparent descendant of her family, and some sources, Mahidevran was one of the daughters of Idar of Kabardia, a 16th-century Kabardian prince who was allegedly married to Nazcan Hatun, daughter of Meñli I Giray, and her birth name was Malhurub Idarovna. This interview supports the theory of a Circassian origin, and according to some scholars, she was the sister of Makhoshoqo Qanoqo, and according to one source, she was originally named Rosne Pravane and was the daughter of Abdullah Recai, a wealthy Albanian musician who allegedly gave her to the palace, or she may simply have been kidnapped in one of the many Ottoman raids. Because there is no clear contemporary record about her birthplace or family, scholars continue to debate this issue. Mahidevran was one of the seventeen women in the harem of Suleiman when he served as governor of Manisa. According to stipend records, three women ranked above her and received 5 aspers a day, while Mahidevran and two others received 4 aspers per day. This shows that although she was not the highest-ranking woman at that time, she still held an important position. The exact religion of Mahidevran Hatun prior to her conversion to Islam is not documented in contemporary Ottoman sources. She is widely believed to have been of Circassian origin. In the early 16th century, many Circassians adhered either to traditional indigenous beliefs or to Eastern Orthodox Christianity, as the large-scale Islamization of Circassia occurred in later centuries. Like other women who entered the Ottoman imperial harem, Mahidevran converted to Islam upon her inclusion in the imperial household. Within the harem there were also two concubines, Akile Hatun and Belkis Hatun, who acted as Mahidevran’s handmaidens. They were buried in one of the mausoleums of the Muradiye complex in Bursa, near Mahidevran. Some later writers have suggested that they were her elder sisters. However, it is more likely that they were girls brought to the harem at the same time as Mahidevran and later entered her service when she became a favored concubine. In 1515, Mahidevran gave birth to her only child, Şehzade Mustafa. The birth of a son greatly increased her status in the harem. When Sultan Selim I died in 1520 and Suleiman became sultan, Mahidevran moved to the Old Palace in Constantinople. As the mother of a prince, she now held a strong and respected position. In 1521, Suleiman’s two older sons, Mahmud and Murad, died. After their deaths, Mustafa became the eldest surviving prince of Suleiman’s generation. This made Mahidevran even more important within the palace hierarchy. Being the mother of the eldest prince gave her political influence and prestige. However, early in Suleiman’s reign, Mahidevran faced a powerful rival: Hürrem. Hürrem soon became Suleiman’s favorite concubine and later his legal wife. According to the Venetian ambassador Bernardo Navagero, Suleiman at first valued both Mahidevran and Hürrem. But over time, Mahidevran began to lose favor, especially by 1526, as reported by Bragadin. Navagero reported that a serious quarrel broke out between the two women. During this conflict, Mahidevran reportedly beat and humiliated Hürrem, which angered Suleiman. Mahidevran was described as “the Circassian, naturally proud and beautiful.” She believed that as the mother of the eldest prince and as a woman who had served the sultan before Hürrem, she deserved authority over the other women in the harem. Historian Leslie Peirce accepts that such an incident may have occurred but suggests that the story may have been exaggerated. She notes that the strict rules and discipline of the imperial harem would have limited open violence. Still, Peirce considers it possible that Mahidevran reacted strongly because she felt her senior status was being challenged. The conflict can be understood as part of the intense competition for influence and security within the palace. According to Peirce, Mahidevran’s actions may have been a form of self-defense against the loss of her rank and position. The rivalry between Mahidevran and Hürrem was partly controlled by Hafsa Sultan, Suleiman’s mother. As the Valide Sultan, Hafsa held great authority and likely tried to maintain balance within the harem. However, by 1526 Suleiman had largely turned his attention away from Mahidevran and devoted himself to Hürrem. Despite losing Suleiman’s personal affection, Mahidevran still remained in a respected position because she was the mother of Mustafa, the eldest surviving prince. Suleiman also ensured that she and Mustafa continued to live in comfort. The Venetian ambassador Pietro Bragadin wrote that while they were living in the imperial palace in Istanbul, Mustafa was his mother’s “whole joy.” In summary, although Mahidevran eventually lost Suleiman’s favor to Hürrem, her role as the mother of Şehzade Mustafa secured her lasting importance within the Ottoman dynasty. Her life in the palace reflects both the privileges and the intense rivalries of the imperial harem. Mahidevran Hatun was one of the chief consorts of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent and the mother of Şehzade Mustafa. Some historians consider her to have been Haseki Sultan before the rise of Hürrem Sultan, while others note that the formal title of Haseki was likely established with Hurrem, making Mahidevran’s status debated. As a chief consort, Mahidevran managed her household, controlled estates, and maintained her son’s position as heir apparent. She had social prestige, authority over palace women, and the ability to sponsor charitable works and provincial projects. Although her influence declined after Hürrem Sultan became Suleiman’s favored consort, Mahidevran retained her wealth and continued her charitable and sponsoring activities for the rest of her life. In Ottoman tradition, all princes were expected to serve as provincial governors (Sanjak-bey) to gain experience in ruling before they could inherit the throne. In 1533, Mustafa was sent to Manisa for this purpose, and Mahidevran accompanied him. She led Mustafa's princely harem and oversaw his household. From the start, Mahidevran worked to protect her son from potential political rivals and threats, maintaining influence and likely a network of informants to keep him safe. Foreign ambassadors, especially from the Venetian Republic, closely followed Ottoman dynastic affairs. Their reports often mentioned Mahidevran and give a clear sense of the critical role a prince’s mother played in ensuring his security and success. Mahidevran’s presence at Mustafa’s side was considered essential; she managed his household and guided his decisions, helping him gain support from officials, soldiers, and other influential figures. The grand vizier Pargalı Ibrahim Pasha was a strong supporter of Mustafa. Letters between the pasha, Mahidevran, and Mustafa show close and affectionate relationships. In her correspondence with the grand vizier, Mahidevran expressed gratitude for his guidance and emphasized the trust, loyalty, and friendship that existed between them. Around 1540, Bassano, a foreign observer, described Mustafa’s court in Diyarbakır, near the Safavid border, as "most wonderful and glorious, no less than that of his father." He also noted that "his mother, who was with him, instructs him in how to make himself loved by the people." In 1541, Mustafa was transferred to Amasya, another important province for training princes. By 1546, three other sons of Suleiman were also serving as governors, and competition for succession began to grow among the four princes, although Suleiman would live for another twenty years. Mahidevran continued to watch over Mustafa, protecting him from rivals and guiding him through the complex politics of the court. In a report from 1553, ambassador Bernado Navagero described Mahidevran’s careful efforts to safeguard Mustafa: "Mustafa has with him his mother, who exercises great diligence to guard him from poisoning and reminds him every day that he has nothing else but this to avoid, and it is said that he has boundless respect and reverence for her." Mustafa was an extremely popular prince. Even as a child, foreign observers noted his extraordinary talent. The Venetian ambassador wrote that "he will be a warrior, is much loved by the Janissaries, and performs great feats." By 1553, Navagero added, "It is impossible to describe how much he is loved and desired by all as successor to the throne." During Suleiman’s long reign, rivalry among his sons became a source of tension. Rumors suggested that both Hürrem Sultan and the grand vizier Rüstem Pasha tried to turn the sultan against Mustafa, accusing him of stirring unrest. However, there is no definitive evidence of such a conspiracy. In 1553, during the campaign against Safavid Persia, Suleiman ordered the execution of Mustafa on charges of plotting to overthrow his father. Historians have never been able to prove or disprove Mustafa’s guilt. On the day of the execution, the ambassador Trevisano reported that Mahidevran had sent a messenger to warn Mustafa of his father’s intentions. Unfortunately, Mustafa ignored the message, consistently refusing to listen to warnings from his friends and even from his mother. Mahidevran’s attempts to save her son illustrate both her courage and the precarious position of women in the Ottoman dynastic system. Despite her high status as mother of the eldest surviving prince, she could not prevent the political forces arrayed against Mustafa. Mahidevran remained loyal to Mustafa until the end. She worked tirelessly to protect him, advise him, and maintain his safety. Foreign accounts show that she played a critical role in his administration, ensuring he was loved by the people, supported by officials, and respected by the military. Even after Mustafa’s death, her reputation as a devoted mother and political actor in the Ottoman court remained widely acknowledged in contemporary records. Mahidevran’s political role was closely tied to her position as the mother of Şehzade Mustafa, the eldest son of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent. In the Ottoman Empire, being the mother of the sultan’s eldest son gave her an important place in the palace and in state politics. From the moment Mustafa was born, Mahidevran’s influence depended on her ability to protect and support him as the future ruler. In the early 1530s, Mahidevran began actively working to secure her son’s position. She built alliances with palace officials, provincial governors, and military leaders who supported Mustafa. These alliances were important because the Ottoman court was full of rival groups. Many people tried to influence the sultan and gain power for themselves or their children. One of Mahidevran’s key strategies was to ensure that Mustafa was given important provinces to govern. Ottoman princes were trained in provincial rule before they could become sultan. Mustafa was sent to Manisa and Amasya, provinces that were both politically and militarily important. Being in these provinces helped Mustafa gain experience in ruling, controlling armies, and building support from local leaders. Mahidevran worked to keep him safe and popular in these regions. Mahidevran also used her position to influence what happened inside the palace. She was in direct competition with Hürrem Sultan, another consort of Suleiman. Hürrem wanted her own sons to become sultan, which meant that she and Mahidevran were rivals. Mahidevran tried to counter Hürrem by forming a network of supporters inside the palace. This included palace staff, officials, eunuchs, and even some soldiers who favored Mustafa. Their rivalry was not just personal — it affected important decisions about government, military, and provincial appointments. During the 1530s and 1540s, Mahidevran’s influence was strong because Mustafa was seen as the main heir. She advised her son, helped him build support, and guided his decisions in his provinces. Many governors and military leaders listened to her advice because they respected Mustafa and wanted to support him. Her influence reached both the palace and the wider Ottoman Empire. However, Hürrem Sultan’s rise changed the balance of power. By having multiple sons and winning Suleiman’s trust, Hürrem became more powerful. This made it harder for Mahidevran to protect Mustafa and her own influence inside the palace. Over time, Hürrem’s faction gained control of key positions and reduced Mahidevran’s political power. Mahidevran tried different strategies to maintain her power. She continued to build alliances with governors and military leaders who were loyal to Mustafa. She also tried to influence Suleiman’s decisions by emphasizing Mustafa’s popularity and experience. These efforts show that she was an intelligent and skilled political actor, even in a court dominated by another powerful woman. Her role in politics was not only about protecting her son. It also affected the Ottoman Empire as a whole. Succession in the Ottoman Empire was very important because disputes over the throne could lead to rebellions or weaken the state. By supporting Mustafa, Mahidevran played a part in keeping the empire stable. Foreign powers also watched Ottoman succession carefully, so her actions had indirect effects on diplomacy and military planning. Even after Hürrem became very powerful, Mahidevran remained politically active. She continued to manage her estates and use her wealth to support her allies. She also tried to maintain the loyalty of Mustafa’s supporters in the provinces and in the army. This shows that her political influence was not limited to the palace but extended to the empire’s wider administration. The rivalry between Mahidevran and Hürrem eventually ended with the tragic execution of Mustafa in 1553. This marked the loss of her main political power. However, historians note that her efforts over two decades show the important role that women could play in Ottoman politics. Even without a formal title, Mahidevran influenced decisions at the highest levels of government, shaped succession politics, and managed alliances that affected the empire. In summary, Mahidevran’s political life was defined by her position as mother of the heir, her alliances with officials and military leaders, and her long rivalry with Hürrem Sultan. Her story demonstrates how Ottoman women could exert significant influence in court politics, succession, and governance, even without holding formal office. Through her support of Mustafa, she affected both domestic and foreign affairs, leaving a lasting legacy in Ottoman history. Mahidevran was one of the richest women in the Ottoman Empire. Her wealth was mainly because she was the mother of Şehzade Mustafa, the eldest son of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent. In the Ottoman system, the mother of a prince could receive lands, estates, gifts, and money from the sultan. These resources allowed her to live comfortably, maintain a large household, and support her allies. Most of Mahidevran’s wealth came from lands called timars and vakıfs. Timars were lands given by the sultan that produced income from taxes and farming. Vakıfs were religious or charitable lands that also generated money. She received estates in different provinces where Mustafa worked as a governor. The income from these lands helped her run her household and give gifts to loyal officials. Mahidevran also received expensive gifts directly from Sultan Suleiman. These included jewelry, fine clothing, carpets, and other luxurious household items. These gifts were signs of her status in the palace. They also helped her influence officials, palace staff, and other women in the harem. Her wealth allowed her to maintain a large household. She had many servants, guards, cooks, and attendants. Managing this household was expensive, but it also showed her power in the palace. The size and luxury of her household reflected her position as the mother of the heir apparent. Mahidevran used her wealth to build alliances. She gave gifts to palace officials, military leaders, and governors who supported Mustafa. These gifts encouraged loyalty and helped her maintain influence in the court. During Mustafa’s time as governor of Manisa and Amasya, Mahidevran helped manage funds to support his administration. She paid soldiers, rewarded loyal officials, and organized ceremonies. By controlling these resources, she helped ensure her son’s authority was recognized in the provinces. Mahidevran also used her wealth for charity. She donated money to build mosques, fountains, and schools. These acts showed she was pious and generous, and they improved her reputation among the people. After Mustafa’s execution in 1553, Mahidevran kept much of her wealth. She moved to Bursa, where she lived comfortably and continued to manage her estates. Even in retirement, she used her wealth to support her household and remaining allies. Her wealth gave her independence. Unlike many women in the palace who depended entirely on the sultan’s favor, Mahidevran could make decisions about her household and estates. She could reward supporters, manage finances, and continue charitable work without needing approval. Mahidevran’s estates were carefully managed. She appointed trusted officials to collect taxes and manage farms. This ensured that her income was steady and that her influence reached beyond the palace. Her wealth also allowed her to remain involved in succession politics. She could give gifts and support to those loyal to Mustafa. Money became a tool for influence, and her careful management helped her retain authority even after her son’s death. Overall, Mahidevran Hatun’s wealth was not only personal. It gave her independence, influence, and the power to support her son, manage her household, and participate in court life. Her careful use of estates, gifts, and charitable works shows how Ottoman women could wield power through wealth. Mahidevran Hatun played an important role as a sponsor in the Ottoman Empire. She used her wealth to support many local projects, institutions, and skilled workers. Her sponsorship included educational, religious, cultural, and economic initiatives that benefited towns and villages throughout the empire. One of her main areas of sponsorship was education. Mahidevran financed schools where children could learn reading, writing, and religious studies. These schools helped communities gain knowledge and improved the social standing of towns where her projects were active. She sometimes provided salaries for teachers and support for students from poor families, showing her commitment to education. Mahidevran Hatun also sponsored small mosques and fountains. These public works improved daily life by providing clean water and spaces for prayer and community gatherings. While not as grand as larger imperial constructions, these projects were highly valued by local populations and reflected her personal dedication to the welfare of her people. Another aspect of her sponsorship was the support of artisans, craftsmen, and local tradespeople. She financed skilled workers and encouraged the production of fine crafts, textiles, and other goods. By investing in these professions, she helped maintain local economies and promote skilled labor, which in turn strengthened her influence in the provinces. Mahidevran also sponsored provincial governors and officials by providing funds for public works, administration, and infrastructure projects. This allowed local leaders to maintain order, repair roads, and build smaller bridges and public spaces. Her financial support reinforced loyalty among administrators and extended her influence beyond the palace walls. In addition to material support, Mahidevran sponsored religious scholars and writers. She encouraged the production of manuscripts and the preservation of religious texts. By supporting scholars, she contributed to the intellectual and cultural life of the empire, while also reinforcing her image as a pious and educated patron. Her sponsorship was closely linked to her political influence. By providing funds and resources, Mahidevran could gain support from local officials, craftsmen, and religious leaders. These alliances helped her maintain a strong presence in both the palace and the provinces, even after the death of her son Mustafa. Through her sponsorship, Mahidevran Hatun demonstrated how Ottoman women could exercise soft power. Her wealth was not only used for personal luxury but also to improve society, culture, and local governance. By funding schools, fountains, mosques, artisans, and provincial projects, she left a lasting impact on the communities she supported. Overall, Mahidevran’s role as a sponsor shows that Ottoman royal women could influence society through wealth and patronage. Her support of education, religious institutions, skilled labor, and local governance reflects a deliberate strategy to maintain influence, improve her reputation, and contribute to the welfare of the empire. After the execution of her son, Mahidevran lived a difficult and poor life for many years. She moved to Bursa, where her son Şehzade Mustafa was buried. Mahidevran became the last of Suleiman’s concubines to retire to Bursa. Unlike some of her predecessors who had remained wealthy and influential, Mahidevran struggled financially. She could not even pay the rent on her house, and her servants were often mocked, cheated, or harassed in local markets. Years after Mustafa’s death, Mahidevran sought to return to the palace. She asked Yahya Efendi, a close friend and milk brother of Sultan Suleiman, to intercede on her behalf. However, Suleiman saw this request as bold and disrespectful, and he dismissed Yahya from his teaching position. This left Mahidevran in a state of social and financial insecurity for a long time. Her situation improved around 1573, nearly twenty years after Mustafa’s death. By then, Sultan Selim II, who had become sultan in 1566, paid off her debts and purchased a house for her. With this support, Mahidevran regained some stability and dignity. At the same time, her son Mustafa finally received a proper burial. Earlier, after his death in Konya Ereğlisi in 1553, Mustafa’s body had been moved to Bursa and buried elsewhere. Now, a proper tomb was built for him by Mehmed Çavuş, allowing Mahidevran to honor him appropriately. With her finances secured, Mahidevran also created an endowment to maintain her son’s tomb. This shows that she remained deeply devoted to Mustafa even after many years of hardship. She continued to live in Bursa until her death on 3 February 1581. She outlived Sultan Suleiman and all of his children, witnessing nearly three decades after Mustafa’s death. Mahidevran was buried in the same tomb as her son. The mausoleum contains four coffins: that of Şehzâde Mustafa, Mahidevran herself, an unknown child (possibly one of Mustafa’s sons who had been executed), and Şehzâde Osman, who was likely a son of Sultan Bayezid II and died in 1512 or 1513. This makes Şehzâde Osman’s tomb the oldest in the mausoleum. Even in her later years, Mahidevran’s life reflects the challenges faced by women in the Ottoman imperial family. Once a favored concubine and mother of the eldest prince, she experienced loss, financial hardship, and the consequences of palace politics. Yet she remained devoted to her son until her last days, ensuring his memory and tomb were preserved with care. Her story highlights both the vulnerability and resilience of women in the Ottoman harem system, as well as the political importance of a prince’s mother. After the death of her son Şehzade Mustafa in 1553, Mahidevran Hatun lived a quieter life compared to her earlier years in the palace. When Murad III became sultan in 1574, she was already older and living mostly in Bursa, away from the central court in Istanbul. During this time, Mahidevran focused on managing her estates and maintaining her household. She continued to live comfortably thanks to the income from her lands and vakıfs, and she retained influence in local matters through her wealth. Although she no longer played an active role in palace politics, Mahidevran maintained her social presence through charitable works and sponsorships. She donated to schools, mosques, and local projects, which allowed her to remain respected among the people and officials in the provinces. Her later life was marked by a degree of independence unusual for women of her time. She could manage her own finances, make decisions about her household, and continue charitable activities without needing approval from the sultan or the court. Mahidevran Hatun eventually passed away sometime during the late 16th century, leaving behind a legacy of wealth, charity, and influence that continued to be remembered by the Ottoman elite. After Mahidevran's death, she continued to be remembered in Ottoman history as a woman of influence, wealth, and generosity. In many chronicles and local accounts, she was referred to as Mahidevran Hatun, reflecting her historical identity as the mother of Şehzade Mustafa and a respected figure of the imperial family. Her estates and endowments continued to provide income for charitable works, schools, and religious institutions that she had supported during her life. Historians noted her ability to manage wealth, sponsor education, and support artisans and provincial officials, highlighting a legacy that extended beyond palace intrigue and rivalries. Even in death, Mahidevran Hatun’s contributions to education, religion, and local economies remained visible. The schools, fountains, mosques, and charitable foundations she had sponsored continued to serve communities for decades, ensuring that her influence outlasted her lifetime. Ottoman historians often cited her as an example of how royal women could wield social and cultural power through wealth and patronage, even if they were not formally involved in state governance. Mahidevran Hatun’s death marked the conclusion of a life that combined personal struggle, courtly rivalry, and substantial social influence. Nevertheless, her careful management of estates, continued charitable works, and sponsorship of education and skilled labor ensured that her memory endured and that her legacy as a capable, influential Ottoman royal woman remained firmly established. Mahidevran Hatun, historically referred to as Mahidevran Sultan, occupied a distinguished position in the Ottoman imperial hierarchy during the early reign of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent. Her honours were closely linked to her status as one of the Sultan’s principal consorts and, most importantly, as the mother of his eldest son, Şehzade Mustafa. Although some historical sources suggest she may have been formally recognized as Haseki Sultan during the early years of Suleiman’s reign, others argue that she was more accurately referred to as Hatun, a designation denoting her high rank within the imperial harem without necessarily implying the exclusive privileges of a Haseki. As a principal consort, Mahidevran Hatun enjoyed a status that conferred both ceremonial and social privileges. She was granted precedence over other women in the harem and was entitled to maintain her own household within the palace complex. Her role as a consort included oversight of palace ceremonies, participation in official events, and the ability to sponsor servants, attendants, and minor courtiers. These honours, while not codified in the sense of a formal title or medal, reflected the intricate hierarchy and ceremonial protocol of the Ottoman court, where rank and recognition were conveyed through residence, access, and privilege rather than written decree. Her status was further enhanced by her position as mother of Şehzade Mustafa. The Ottoman imperial system placed significant honour upon the mother of the Sultan’s eldest son, as such women were regarded as protectors and guides of potential heirs. This honour was both practical and symbolic: it granted Mahidevran influence within the harem, access to key courtly figures, and a recognized role in matters concerning the upbringing and education of her son. While her influence was largely exercised indirectly, through her son, it nonetheless represented a tangible form of recognition within the Ottoman court’s intricate social hierarchy. Even after the decline of her political influence with the rise of Hürrem Sultan, Mahidevran retained certain honours by virtue of her rank and her continued recognition as the mother of a prominent prince. She was accorded respect in ceremonial occasions, continued to maintain her household, and was recognized as a figure of historical note in the court’s social memory. These honours, though largely symbolic in her later years, illustrate the persistence of courtly recognition independent of direct political power. Mahidevran Hatun’s honours also extended to her residence and estates. Following her withdrawal from central court life, she managed her properties in Bursa, where her status as a former principal consort and mother of a prince ensured deference and recognition from local officials, scholars, and notable families. The management of estates and the maintenance of a household in accordance with courtly customs were themselves considered a form of honour in the Ottoman context, reflecting the continued social prominence of former consorts even after their retreat from political affairs. Throughout her life, Mahidevran’s honours were inseparable from the hierarchical and ceremonial structures of the Ottoman court. They were conveyed not only through titles but through precedence in the harem, recognition in courtly events, access to the Sultan and his advisors, and the respect accorded to her as the mother of a prominent prince. The combination of these honours constituted a multifaceted recognition of her rank, influence, and social standing, and they remained notable even after her direct involvement in imperial politics diminished. Despite the eventual overshadowing by Hürrem Sultan and the execution of Şehzade Mustafa, Mahidevran Hatun’s honours persisted as markers of her former prominence. Historical accounts emphasize that she retained recognition as a woman of the imperial household, reflecting the ways in which honours in the Ottoman system were linked not only to political power but also to birth, maternal role, and ceremonial position. Her continued acknowledgment in both palace records and social memory underscores the enduring nature of these honours, which were less ephemeral than political influence and served as a testament to her historical significance. In summary, Mahidevran’s honours encompassed her recognition as a principal consort, her ceremonial precedence within the harem, her status as mother of Şehzade Mustafa, and her continued prominence in Bursa following her retreat from court life. While she may not have received formal titles or awards in the modern sense, the honours conferred upon her reflect the Ottoman system of courtly recognition, where rank, maternal status, household management, and ceremonial precedence collectively constituted a form of lasting acknowledgement of a woman’s importance within the imperial structure. Mahidevran Hatun occupies a distinctive place in Ottoman history, remembered as a principal consort of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent and as the mother of Şehzade Mustafa. Her legacy is multifaceted, reflecting her role in the succession politics of the sixteenth century, her enduring social and cultural influence, and the ways in which historical memory has preserved her life story. Referred to in contemporary and later sources as 'Mahidevran Hatun', she exemplifies the complexities of status, honour, and influence for women within the Ottoman imperial system. Mahidevran Hatun’s historical prominence is closely tied to the life and fate of her son, Şehzade Mustafa. As the mother of the Sultan’s eldest surviving son, she was positioned at the center of the court’s succession politics. Mustafa’s position as heir apparent gave Mahidevran Hatun a measure of prestige and recognition, and her maternal authority was acknowledged both within the harem and indirectly in broader political circles. Her influence was exercised through her son, through courtly ceremonies, and through networks of patronage that linked her to officials, provincial governors, and military leaders who supported Mustafa’s position. In this context, Mahidevran Hatun’s legacy is inseparable from her role as mother, which provided her with both status and visibility within the Ottoman imperial hierarchy. The execution of Şehzade Mustafa in 1553 marked a profound turning point in Mahidevran Hatun’s life and legacy. Contemporary sources recount that she suffered greatly as a result of her son’s death, which simultaneously ended his prospects for succession and reduced her own influence at court. Despite this personal and political setback, Mahidevran Hatun maintained her dignity and continued to command respect, relocating to Bursa where she managed her estates and household. Her ability to retain social prominence even after the loss of her son illustrates the enduring recognition she enjoyed as a former principal consort and as a woman of high rank within the Ottoman hierarchy. Mahidevran Hatun is frequently contrasted with Hürrem Sultan in historical narratives, which has shaped perceptions of her legacy. While Hürrem is celebrated for her exceptional political influence and access to the Sultan, Mahidevran Hatun is remembered for her resilience, dignity, and maternal devotion. Historians note that she experienced the apex of imperial favour, only to face marginalization later in life, a trajectory that underscores the precariousness of power within the harem and the court at large. This juxtaposition has contributed to a narrative framing Mahidevran Hatun as a tragic yet notable figure, whose life exemplifies both the opportunities and limitations faced by women in the Ottoman imperial system. During her residence in Bursa, Mahidevran Hatun continued to exert social influence and maintain her recognition as a member of the royal household. Her estates functioned as centers for cultural and social activity, demonstrating that former consorts could retain authority and honour outside the immediate sphere of court politics. Through her management of properties, patronage of local institutions, and ceremonial recognition in provincial society, Mahidevran Hatun’s legacy extended beyond the palace, highlighting the ways in which women of her rank continued to shape Ottoman society even after retreating from central political life. The historiographical record has preserved Mahidevran Hatun as a symbol of maternal devotion and resilience. Chroniclers often emphasize her care for Şehzade Mustafa, her attempts to safeguard his education and position, and her dignified conduct following his execution. Such portrayals contribute to a legacy that balances recognition of social and political influence with acknowledgment of personal hardship, reflecting the multidimensional nature of her life and the lasting historical interest in her story. In addition to historical accounts, Mahidevran Hatun’s life has been represented in cultural and literary contexts. In historical novels, television series, and scholarly discussions, she is depicted as a figure of strength, endurance, and, at times, tragedy. These representations, while sometimes dramatized, reinforce the enduring fascination with her life and the circumstances that shaped her influence within the Ottoman imperial household. Mahidevran Hatun’s legacy also provides insights into the broader roles of women in Ottoman succession politics and court life. Her experiences demonstrate how maternal authority, ceremonial recognition, and social networks functioned as forms of enduring influence. Even when formal power waned, her continued recognition in provincial society and her management of estates illustrate the mechanisms through which women maintained status and exerted agency. Scholars have emphasized that her life challenges simplistic narratives of women’s power, highlighting the interplay of personal resilience, maternal devotion, and structural limitations within the imperial household. The debates surrounding her designation as Haseki Sultan versus Hatun further underscore the historiographical significance of her legacy. These discussions inform modern understanding of Ottoman court hierarchy, ceremonial rank, and the influence of women within the palace. By examining Mahidevran Hatun’s life and recognition, historians explore the nuanced ways in which status, honour, and influence were conveyed, demonstrating that her legacy extends beyond personal biography to contribute to the study of Ottoman imperial structures. Moreover, Mahidevran Hatun’s life has been a subject of comparative studies, particularly in the context of dynastic succession and the roles of women in other Islamic courts. Her experiences exemplify how maternal relationships, ceremonial precedence, and social networks served as mechanisms for sustaining influence and honour, even amid the political upheavals of the palace. The continued scholarly and popular interest in her story attests to the enduring relevance of her experiences for understanding gender, power, and social structures in the Ottoman Empire.

Ayatollah Seyyed Mahmoud Hashemi Shahroudi (15 August 1948 – 24 December 2018) was an Iranian politician. He was the Chief Justice of Iran from 1999 to 2009. He was born in Najaf, Iraq. Ayatollah Shahroudi was best known for ordering a moratorium on stoning as a form of the death penalty. However, later it was shown that executions by stoning are still being carried out, in spite of his claims that they have stopped. Stoning is still happening inside prisons, where the public cannot see it. From August 2017 to December 2018, Shahroudi was Chairman of Expediency Discernment Council. He died on 24 December 2018 from cancer in Tehran at the age of 70.

Mahmud I (; August 2, 1696 – December 13, 1754) was the Sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1730 to 1754. He was the son of Mustafa II (1695–1703). His mother Emetullah Sultan, (born as Evemia) was of Greek ethnic descent. Mahmud I was the older brother of Osman III (1754–57).

Mahmud II (Ottoman Turkish: محمود ثاني Mahmud-ı sānī) (July 20, 1785 – July 1, 1839) was the 30th Sultan of the Ottoman Empire. Often described as the "Peter the Great of Turkey", he ruled from 1808 until his death. Mahmud was the son of Sultan Abdul Hamid I. His time as sultan is notable mostly for the major legal and military changes he caused. Mahmud instituted extensive administrative, military, and fiscal reforms. His disbandment of the conservative Janissary corps removed a major obstacle to his and his successors' reforms in the Empire. Mahmud's reign was also marked by further Ottoman military defeat and loss of territory as a result of nationalist uprisings and European intervention. Mahmud II was born in Istanbul. He was 23 years old when he came to the throne. He was an Islamic calligraphy artist, composer and poet. He wrote poems under the pseudonym "Adli". He was of a brave, patient and prudent temperament. He replaced the old military organization maintained by the governors of irregular auxiliaries (sekban - I Cedid). When the soldiers shortly after arose, he defeated them. The 1808 revolting insurgents killed Alemdar Mustafa Pasha. In 1812 the peace treaty was signed in Bucharest with the Russians. In 1813, with the help of Muhammed Ali Pasha, he defeated the Wahhabis, who desecrated the holy places and shrines in Mecca and Medina. In 1821 the Greek War of Independence broke out and thousands were killed. In the “Auspicious Incident” the corps of Janissaries was abolished and replaced by a conscription army. In 1827 the war with Russia began again. In 1829 the peace treaty was concluded in Edirne. In the years 1831 and 1839, riots broke out in Egypt. In July of 1839 the Sultan Mahmud II died as the ill effects of life experienced by him calamitous events he was afflicted with tuberculosis and died. His body was buried in the Türbe in Divanyolu. Mahmud II was devoted to many works of the highest degree in any field. He opened many new schools, and ordered to build large buildings. All the great mosques of Istanbul were repaired in his time. The bridge was built in Unkapani his time. In Mecca, he had built a madrasa and mend the Great Mosque (Mescid-i Aksa) in the holy city of Jerusalem. The poet and Sümbülzâde Vehbi Kececizâde Izzet Molla died at this time. His sons: Abdulmejid I *, * Abdulaziz, 4 Sehzades names Ahmet, Bayezid, veliaht Abdulhamid, Suleyman, 2 Sehzades called Mehmed Murad Nizameddin, Abdullah Osman. His daughters: Emine Sultan, Sultan Hamide, Hayriye Sultan, Sultan Saw, * Saliha Sultan, Ayse Sultan, Sultan Atike *, 2 Fatma Sultan, Sultan Münire, Mihrimah Sultan *, * Adile Sultan.

Mahmud II (Kabızlık; died 1131) proclaimed himself the Seljuk sultan of Baghdad in 1118 after the death of Mehmed I (probably Mahmud's father). Mahmud fought against the Seljuk Sultan of Khorasan, Ahmed Sanjar, whom Mehmed I had revolted against in 1105. Mahmud was succeeded by Dawud.

Mahmud of Ghazni, (, Maḥmūd-e Ghaznawī; (2 November 971 – 30 April 1030) commonly known as Mahmud Ghaznavi, was the ruler of the Ghaznavid Empire from 997 until his death. He turned the former provincial city of Ghazni into the rich capital of an extensive empire which included modern-day Afghanistan, most of Iran, and parts of north-west India including modern-day Pakistan. He was also the first ruler to carry the title Sultan, signifying his break from the power of the Islamic Caliph. Mahmud of Ghazni was known as Yāmīn al-Dawlah Maḥmūd (in full: Yāmīn al-Dawlah Abd al-Qāṣim Maḥmūd ibn Sebük Tegīn). He was the eldest son of Emir Sebüktegin. When he was young, Mahmud helped his father gain land through military campaigns against Turk nobles. In 997, he overthrew his younger brother, Ismail, who had been nominated for the throne after his father’s death. As soon as he had the throne, he went out to conquer territory. Between 1000 and 1026, he invaded India at least 17 times. He led the first major Muslim army to invade India. His conquest of the entire Punjab including Haryana all the way up to Agra was the last invasion where he increased his territory in India. From then on, most of Mahmud’s raids were to gain wealth. Mahmud's last and most famous raid was on Somnath. This is a temple city on the Gujarati coast that was also a pilgrimage site. The temple had many riches: heavy golden chains and thousands of jewels. The battle was violent, and more than 50,000 people died. Mahmud's army won and plundered the temple of its riches and wealth. With all his riches, Mahmud founded a university, a library, and a museum, a grand mosque and richened his capital. When Mahmud was about to die, he ordered all of his riches to be placed before him. Mahmud died on 30 April 1030. 994: Gains the title of Saif ad-Dawla and becomes Governor of Khorasan under service to NuhII of the Samanid Empire in civil strife 995: The Samanid rebels Fa'iq (leader of a court faction that had defeated Alptigin's nomination for Emir) and Abu Ali expel Mahmud from Nishapur. Mahmud and Sabuktigin defeat Samanid rebels at Tus 999: Khorasan, Balkh, Herat, Merv from the Samanids. A concurrent invasion from the north by the Qarakhanids under Elik Khan (Nasr Khan) ends Samanid rule. 1001: Gandhara: Sultan Mahmud defeats Raja Jayapala in the Battle of Peshawar; Jayapala subsequently abdicates and commits suicide. 1004: Bhatia (Bhera) is annexed after it fails to pay its yearly tribute. 1005-6: Multan: Fateh Daud, the Ismaili ruler of Multan revolts and enlists the aid of Anandapala. Mahmud massacres the Ismailis of Multan in the course of his conquest. Anandapala is defeated at Peshawar and pursued to Sodra (Wazirabad) in modern day Gujranwala and the region is partly annexed by Mahmud. Mahmud then goes on to capture Bathinda from its ruler, Sukhapala. Ghor and Muhammad ibn Suri are then captured by Mahmud, made prisoner along with Muhammad ibn Suri's son, and taken to Ghazni, where Muhammad ibn Suri dies. Appoints Sewakpal to administer the region. Anandapala flees to Kashmir, fort in the hills on the western border of Kashmir. Mehmud attacks the fort but fails to capture it so he destroys every village in Kashmir during his retreat back to Afghanistan. He also defeats an army near Mirpur and captures the area appointing a Muslim governor. He establishes a caravan in the modern day city of Rawalpindi and fully annexes the Pothohar region. 1005: Defends Balkh and Khorasan against NasrI of the Kara-Khanid Khanate and recaptures Nishapur from Isma'il Muntasir of the Samanids. 1005: Sewakpal rebels and is defeated. 1008: Mahmud defeats the Indian Confederacy (Ujjain, Gwalior, Kalinjar, Kannauj, Delhi, and Ajmer) in the Battle of Chach near Hazro in Chach, and captures the Shahi treasury at Kangra, Himachal Pradesh and appoints a governor. Note: A historical narrative states in this battle, under the onslaught of the Gakhars, Mahmud's army was about to retreat when King Anandapala's elephant took flight and turned the tide of the battle. 1010: Multan revolts. It's Ismaili ruler Abul Fatah Dawood is defeated and imprisoned for life at Ghazni. 1012: Invades Gharchistan and deposes its ruler Abu Nasr Muhammad. 1012: Demands and receives remainder of the province of Khorasan from the Abbasid Caliph. Then demands Samarkand as well but is rebuffed. 1013: Bulnat: Defeats Trilochanpala. 1015: Mahmud's army sacks Lahore, but his expedition to Kashmir fails, due to inclement weather. 1015: Khwarezm: Marries his sister to Abul Abbas Mamun of Khwarezm, who dies in the same year in a rebellion. Moves to quell the rebellion and installs a new ruler and annexes a portion. 1017: Kannauj, Meerut, and Muhavun on the Yamuna, Mathura and various other regions along the route. While moving through Kashmir he levies troops from vassal Princes for his onward march; Kannauj and Meerut submit without battle. 1018-1020: Sacks the town of Mathura. 1021: Raises Ayaz to kingship, awarding him the throne of Lahore. 1021: Kalinjar attacks Kannauj: he marches to their aid and finds the last Shahi King, Trilochanpaala, encamped as well. No battle, the opponents leave their baggage trains and withdraw from the field. Also fails to take the fort of Lokote again. Takes Lahore on his return. Trilochanpala flees to Ajmer. First Muslim governors appointed east of the Indus River. 1023: Lahore. He forces Kalinjar and Gwalior to submit and pay tribute: Trilochanpala, the grandson of Jayapala, is assassinated by his own troops. Official annexation of Punjab (including present day Haryana at that time) by Mahmud Ghaznavi. Also fails to take the Lohara fort on the western border of Kashmir for the second time. 1024: Ajmer, Nehrwala, Kathiawar: This raid is his last major campaign. The concentration of wealth at Somnath was renowned, and consequently it became an attractive target for Mahmud, as it had previously deterred most invaders. The temple and citadel are sacked, and most of its defenders massacred. 1025: Somnath: Mahmud sacks the temple and is reported to have personally hammered the temple's gilded Lingam to pieces, and the stone fragments are carted back to Ghazni, where they are incorporated into the steps of the city's new Jama Masjid (Friday Mosque) in 1026. He places a new king on the throne in Gujarat as a tributary. His return detours across the Thar Desert to capture the city of Ajmer and other important forts on his return. 1025: Marches against the Jats of the Jood mountains who harry his army on its return from the sack of Somnath. 1027: Rey, Isfahan, Hamadan from the Buyids Dynasty. 1027: Devastates the fleet of Jats in Indus river to avenge the "heavy losses" suffered by his army in an onslaught by Jats in 1026 CE. 1028, 1029: Merv, Nishapur are lost to the Seljuk dynasty.

Mahmud Shah Durrani (1769 - 1829) was the ruler of the Durrani Empire between 1801 and 1803, again between 1809 and 1818. He was the son of Timur Shah Durrani and half-brother of his predecessor, Zaman Shah. On July 25, 1801, Zaman Shah was deposed, and Mahmud Shah ascended to rulership. He then had a chequered career; he was deposed in 1803, restored in 1809, and finally deposed again in 1818. He died in 1829. Between his two stints, the country was ruled by Shoja Shah, another of his half-brothers.

Mahmoud Fahmi an-Nukrashi Pasha (1888 - 1948) (Arabic: محمود فهمي النقراشي باشا) was an Egyptian political figure. He was the Prime Minister of Egypt from 1945 to 1946 and again from 1946 to 1948. He was assassinated by the Muslim Brotherhood while he was Prime Minister.

Mahmoud Riad (January 8, 1917 – January 25, 1992) was an Egyptian diplomat. He was Egyptian ambassador to United Nations from 1962 to 1964, Egyptian Minister of Foreign Affairs from 1964 to 1972, and Secretary-General of the League of Arab States from 1972 to 1979.: Honorary Commander of the Order of the Defender of the Realm (1965)

Mahmoud Sadeghi is an Iranian lawyer, jurist, academic and reformist politician. He is a member of the Parliament of Iran representing Tehran, Rey, Shemiranat and Eslamshahr electoral district. On 25 February 2020, during the 2019–20 coronavirus pandemic, Sadeghi tested positive for SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes coronavirus disease 2019.

Mahmoud al-Ayyubi (1932 – 11 October 2013) was a Syrian politician. He was Prime Minister of Syria from 21 December 1972 to 7 August 1976 under the presidency of Hafez Al-Asad. He also was Vice President of Syria from February 1971 to August 1976.

Mahmoud Jibril el-Warfally (; 28 May 1952 – 5 April 2020) was a Libyan politician. He served as the interim Prime Minister of Libya for seven and a half months as the executive board of the National Transitional Council from 5 March to 23 October 2011. He was also the Minister of Foreign Affairs. He held these posts during the during the Libyan Civil War in 2011. From 2012 until his death, he was the leader of the National Forces Alliance. He was born in Benghazi. On 5 April 2020, during the 2019–20 coronavirus pandemic, Jibril died in Cairo, Egypt of COVID-19. He was 67.

Mahmoud Refaat (; born April 25, 1978) is an expert in international law, foreign policy advisor (president of European Institute for International Law and International Relations) and writer (a member of the British Association of Journalists – BAJ and the American National Writers Union – NWR in New York) and chairman of the International Gazette daily newspaper based in London, United Kingdom. He is a French-Belgian citizen of Egyptian origin residing between France, Belgium, and the United Kingdom. Mahmoud Refaat led the presidential campaign of former Egyptian army chief of staff Lieutenant General Sami Anan from abroad and played a role in covering all the international media news of the arrest of General Sami Anan, which he explained in several televised meetings that he did so for fear of assassination of Lieutenant General Sami Anan. He then played a role again by questioning international circles in the presidential elections won by Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi in the second round in March 2018, and sparked an international outcry two months later, accusing the Egyptian regime of El-Sisi of trying to assassinate General Sami Anan after the sudden health collapse, that hit him in his prison in summer 2018. Mahmoud Refaat and former Libyan Prime Minister Omar al-Hassi founded The International action group for peace in Libya and he took over the position of General Coordinator, which was launched from the Tunisian capital at a press conference on 12 May 2018 in the presence of a number of the European Parliament and received extensive media coverage. He also played a role in the Yemeni affairs at the international level to urge the international community to ensure the delivery of food and medical aids to civilians, especially those trapped and victims of the Saudi-Emirati bombing and announced that President Abd Rabbu Mansour Hadi must be brought to the International Criminal Court. The International action group for peace in Libya was founded in May 2018 by the former prime minister of Libya, Mr Omar al-Hassi and Dr. Mahmoud Refaat with numerous international personalities from Europe and the international community. Mr Omar al-Hassi is the president and Mahmoud Refaat is the general coordinator of the International action group for peace in Libya. The International Peace Action Group in Libya was founded by Mr. Omar al-Hassi and Mahmoud Refaat through the Middle East and Mediterranean peace Research Institute(MEMPRI) with objectives of helping civilians to avoid results of the War in Libya and also to communicate with the International Community to find the exit of the Civil war led by Haftar and supported by Saudi Arabia and United Arab Emirates. In March 2019, Mahmoud Refaat created The Humanitarian Action Group for Yemen through the European Institute for International Law and International Relations intending to ensure food and medical equipment to civilians in Yemen who are surrounded by the coalition of Saudi Arabia and United Arab Emirates also to work close to the International Community to put an end to the war in Yemen and sue the actors of Yemeni war. The Humanitarian Action Group for Yemen has been urging the International Criminal Court and the International Community to follow war criminals in Yemen, in particular, after several reports from United Nations bodies describe Yemen as worst crises on the earth because of the illegitimate war led by Saudi Arabia and United Arab Emirates on Yemen. Earlier 2019, Mahmoud Refaat announced Mohammad bin Salman and Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan must be trailed as war criminals for their rule of crises in Yemen which left thousands of civilians as victims of starvation, cholera epidemic apart civilians who were killed by the bombing of Saudi-Emirati coalition.

Mahmud Us Samad Chowdhury (মাহমুদ উস সামাদ চৌধুরী) (3 January 1955 – 11 March 2021) was a Bangladeshi politician. He was a member of the Bangladesh Awami League. In 2014, Chowdhury was elected to the Jatiya Sangsad. He was born in Dhaka. Chowdhury died on 11 March 2021 from COVID-19 during the COVID-19 pandemic in Bangladesh in Dhaka, aged 66.

Nāṣiruddīn Maḥmūd Shāh (1435–1459) was the first Sultan of Bengal belonging to the restored Ilyas Shahi dynasty of Bengal sultanate. Formerly a farmer, he was selected as the next ruler of Bengal by the erstwhile nobility in 1435 CE, and ruled the country for over twenty years. During his peaceful reign, Bengal saw significant architectural development.

Maia Grigoryevna Sandu (born 24 May 1972) is a Moldovan politician. Sandu has been the 6th President of Moldova since 24 December 2020. She is the leader of the Party of Action and Solidarity (PAS). She was the Prime Minister of Moldova from 8 June 2019 until 14 November 2019. Sandu was born on 24 May 1972, in the commune of Risipeni, located in the Fălești District in the Moldavian SSR. From 1989 to 1994, she majored in management at the Academy of Economic Studies of Moldavia/Moldova (ASEM). In 2010, she graduated from Harvard University. From 2010 to 2012, Sandu worked as an Adviser to the Executive Director at the World Bank in Washington, D.C.. In June 2019, she became Prime Minister of Moldova. Five months later, on 12 November 2019, Sandu's government fell after the vote of the censure motion. She defeated incumbent president Igor Dodon in the 2020 presidential election. Sandu is the country's first female president. During her presidency, she has been seen as a strong ally of the European Union and Ukraine during the Russian invasion of the country. Sandu has made anti-corruption, economic reform and liberalisation a main part of her political platform. In February 2023, she accused Russia of trying to create a coup of the Moldovan government. In November 2024, Sandu was re-elected in the 2024 election, winning 55% of the vote. In September 2025, his party, PAS, wins the September 2025 legislative elections.

Mai Mala Buni (born 19 November 1967), is a Nigerian politician and the current governor of Yobe state, Nigeria. He is the caretaker chairman of the All Progressives Congress. He was elected governor during the 2019 Nigeria general elections under All Progressives Congress (APC) party. He holds bachelor's degree in International Relation from Espan Formation University, Benin Republic. He also holds a Master's degree in International Relations from Leeds Becket University, United Kingdom. Mala began his political career in 1992 when he contested and won a councilor sit under the platform of National Republican Convention (NRC) party, to represent Buni ward in the Gujba Local government council and subsequently elected as the speaker of the council.

Maina Sage (born 10 May 1975) is a French politician from French Polynesia. She was born in Papeete. She is a member of the Tapura Huiraatira party. Since 2014, she has served as a member of the National Assembly for French Polynesia's 1st constituency. From 2008 to 2017, she was a member of the Assembly of French Polynesia. On 12 March 2020, during the 2019–20 coronavirus pandemic, it was made clear that Sage had tested positive to COVID-19. She became infected after travelling to Paris.

Mairead McGuinness (born 13 June 1959) is an Irish politician. She was the European Commissioner for Financial Stability, Financial Services and the Capital Markets Union from 2020 until 2024. She is a member of Fine Gael. She was First Vice-President of the European Parliament from 2017 to 2020. She was a Member of the European Parliament (MEP) for East from 2004 to 2014 and for Midlands–North-West from 2014 to 2020. McGuinness was Ireland’s longest serving MEP. She ran for President of Ireland in the 2025 presidential election.
Pallewatte Gamaralalage Maithripala Yapa Sirisena (;;; born 3 September 1951) is a Sri Lankan politician and the 7th President of Sri Lanka from January 2015 through November 2019.

Majid Ebn-e-Reza (born 1964) is an Iranian military officer and politician who serves as the acting minister of defense of Iran, since 2 March 2026 after the death of his predecessor Aziz Nasirzadeh on 28 February 2026 during the 2026 Iran War.

Sayyid Hossein Mousavi Eftekhari (, born 17 February 1965) is an Iranian military commander who is the current commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Aerospace Force since 14 June 2025. He is the brigadier general.

Majorian (Latin: Iulius Flavius Valerius Maiorianus, c. 420 - 7 August 461) Was a Western Roman emperor from 1 April 457 - 2 August 461. Majorian was a skilled general and was probably the last hope for the survival of the crumbling Western Roman Empire as he was able to reconquer much of southern gaul and much of Hispania back under Roman Control. In 7 August 461, Majorian was deposed by his friend the germanic roman general Ricimer and was killed. Ricimer and Majorian were really good soldiers and they fought in battle together, and because they were really good, people in the Western Roman Empire. So they killed Avitus, the Roman Emperor. But the thing was, Ricimer was a quite better soldier than Majorian (Majorian was still a skilled soldier), Majorian and Ricimer wanted to become emperor but Ricimer was a foreigner (he was not Roman). So he was not eligible for the Roman throne. So Ricimer had a plan. So when Majorian ascended the throne, he would be the emperor behind the scenes. Majorian became emperor in 457 AD. Ricimer still had his plan still intact. But it did not work because Majorian became too good as emperor. During his reign, Majorian was able to secure several succesful campaigns in Gaul and Hispania reconquering much of both provinces and bringing it back under Roman Control. In 460, Majorian went to Hispania and ordered to build as massive fleet for preperations for an invasion of Africa, but before he was able to put his plans into action, his redied fleet was burned most of it destroyed and only leaving a few warships in a good state. After the incident, Majorian abandons his plans for a possible reconquest of Africa and instead focused on retaking Gaul and Hispania instead. He also replaced the corrupt ruling, which was one of the reasons of the Western Roman Empire falling. Of course Ricimer was mad, he tried to be the "emperor behind the scenes", but already, Majorian conquered those territories. So after he had the war fleets broken, his plan was to betray Majorian by saying secretly to the people that Majorian was unstable to the throne. This was because he became too jealous. In 461, Majorian came to Ricimer without knowing his new plan to talk about new plans for the empire. So he didn’t have any armor. As soon he approached to Ricimer, Ricimer killed his soldiers instantly, and Majorian was deposed and arrested. When Majorian was in jail, he got stripped and got tortured for the next 5 days. In jail, he was questioning, "Why Ricimer?". On August 7 461 AD, he finally got decapitated by Ricimer. Ricimer spread to everybody that Majorian died of natural causes. Ricimer put puppet emperors but nothing worked. Which led to the actual fall of the empire. Ricimer installed a puppet emperor named Libius Severus (Severus III; born in Lucania; died 14 November 465). He was unknown by the Eastern emperor Leo I and by Majorian's soldiers.

Major Claus Enevold Paarss (18 February 1683 – 26 May 1762) was a Danish military officer and official. Retired from service, he was appointed governor of Greenland by King Frederick IV between 1728. Paarss was born in Thy in then Denmark–Norway in 1683 and commanded a Danish man-of-war and threeand 1730. His contingent of colonists consisted of twenty soldiers, three sergeants, and two officers from the Danish artillery corps, along with twelve military convicts, ten unmarried mothers, and two female convicts who were to be wed to one another according to lots. He also carried a dozen horses. Paarss died in Korsør in 1762.

Makarios III, born Michail Christodolou Mouskos (; August 13, 1913 – August 3, 1977), was the archbishop and primate of the autocephalous Cypriot Orthodox Church (1950–1977). He was the first President of the Republic of Cyprus (1960–1974 and 1974–1977). In his three terms as President of Cyprus (1959-1977), he survived four assassination attempts. Makarios died from a heart attack on August 3, 1977 in Nicosia, Cyprus, aged 63.
Maka Bochorishvili (born 15 August 1978) is a Georgian diplomat and politician, Member of Georgian Dream. She is a Member of Parliament of Georgia since 2020.

Makhmut Akhmetovich Gareyev (June 23, 1923 – December 25, 2019) was a Russian General of the Army, a historian, and a military scientist. He was the former Deputy Chief of the General Staff of the Armed Forces of the USSR. He was the president of the Russian Academy of Military Sciences. Gareyev held the Doctor of Science degree in History and Military Science. Gareev was born in Chelyabinsk. He died on December 25, 2019 in Moscow at the age of 96.

Maki Kaji was a Japanese businessman. He was the president of Nikoli. He was known as "the father of Sudoku" for his role in popularizing the number game. He was born in Sapporo, Hokkaido. Kaji died on 10 August 2021 from bile duct cancer in Tokyo, aged 69.

Makebi Zulu (born 25 December 1981) is a Zambian lawyer and politician. He was a Member of Parliament for Malambo Constituency from 2016 to 2021. During this time, he was also the Provincial Minister for Eastern Province. He is a member of the Patriotic Front. In the 2026 Zambian general election, the group he led used the Resolute Party. Zulu was elected to the National Assembly of Zambia in the 2016 general election. He represented Malambo constituency for the Patriotic Front. The following month, he became Eastern Province Minister. In this position, he was responsible for government projects and development work in the province. Zulu also spoke in Parliament about issues such as changes to the Constitution and how the government was run. He also took part in the debate over Bill 10. The bill was proposed in 2019 and led to a national debate. Zulu ran again in Malambo constituency in the 2021 general election. He finished second to Peter Phiri of the United Party for National Development. After the election, Zulu became the lawyer and spokesperson for former President Edgar Lungu and his family. He represented Lungu in a case about whether Lungu could run for president in the 2026 election. He also represented Lungu's family in the legal case about where Lungu would be buried after his death in June 2025. In October 2025, Zulu said that he wanted to become president of the Patriotic Front. On 11 March 2026, the PF Pamodzi Alliance was formed by a group from the PF. Given Lubinda was the acting president of this group. The group then left the Tonse Alliance. On 15 March 2026, Lubinda said that his PF group would hold a convention within four days to choose a new leader. The convention was held online on 21 March 2026. The people who took part elected Makebi Zulu as president of the group. He received 49.2% of the vote. Chitalu Chilufya received 34.1%. At the time, Miles Sampa was recognised as the legal PF president. Because of this, the PF group led by Zulu decided to use another party for the 2026 general election. In early May 2026, the Resolute Party was chosen for this purpose. Later that month, the PF Pamodzi Alliance agreed to work with the Tonse Alliance for the 2026 election. The two groups agreed that Brian Mundubile would be the presidential candidate and Zulu would be his running mate.

Makoto Kobayashi (artist) (born 1958), Japanese manga artist Makoto Kobayashi (physicist) (born 1944), Japanese physicist Makoto Kobayashi (Olympics), President of the Organizing Committee for the 1998 Winter Olympics and Paralympics

Makoto Koga is a Japanese politician. He is a member of the Liberal Democratic Party. He was a member of the House of Representatives in the Diet from 1980 until 2012. He was the Minister of Transport from 1996 to 1997. Koga was born in Fukuoka, Japan.
